paragraphs: This paper investigates how to turn a probabilistic model into features useful for classification. Its starting point is the Fisher kernel, which provides a way to combine probabilistic modeling with discriminative classifiers such as support vector machines. The authors propose a different construction, called the TOP kernel, designed around information that directly concerns class distinctions.

The key difference is the quantity from which the features are derived. The Fisher kernel uses changes in marginal log-likelihood, whereas TOP uses tangent vectors of posterior log-odds. In plain language, TOP describes how the model's relative support for competing classes changes, giving its representation an explicitly discriminative focus.

The paper also develops a theoretical framework for studying feature extractors built from probabilistic models and applies it to both kernels. Experiments favor TOP over the Fisher kernel. These results support the proposed representation in the tested settings, while the theoretical framework makes the relationship between probabilistic modeling and discriminative feature extraction more explicit.
neurips-2001-a-new-discriminative-kernel.tldr: The TOP kernel extracts classification-focused features from posterior log-odds and compares favorably with the Fisher kernel in experiments.

paragraphs: Sparse learning seeks models that make useful predictions while relying on relatively few active components. This paper introduces a prior that encourages such sparseness without requiring its own adjustable or estimated hyperparameters. The central contribution is therefore a way to favor compact models without separately choosing how strongly this prior should encourage sparsity.

The authors focus on supervised regression and classification, although they identify the prior as potentially useful elsewhere. In these tasks, the challenge is to obtain a compact model while retaining predictive accuracy. Evaluating both error rates and sparseness matters because reducing model size alone would not establish that the resulting predictor remains useful.

Experiments on several public benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance. The method outperforms support vector machines and competes with the strongest alternative techniques in both error and sparseness. These are empirical findings for the evaluated tasks. The absence of tuning specifically concerns sparseness-controlling hyperparameters, which is the practical advantage emphasized alongside the reported predictive results.
neurips-2001-adaptive-sparseness-using-j.tldr: A sparsity-inducing prior avoids sparsity hyperparameter tuning while achieving strong benchmark results in regression and classification.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a clustering algorithm for vector quantization, where reference vectors represent groups of input observations. The method uses a stochastic association model to obtain a simple softmax adaptation rule. Its update process closely follows online K-means, making the source of its different behavior particularly specific.

The change is to introduce random fluctuations when evaluating distortion, or how well a reference vector matches an input. The authors emphasize that these fluctuations must be uncorrelated across reference vectors. Randomness therefore enters the comparison process that guides adaptation, rather than being presented merely as an incidental disturbance to otherwise deterministic computation.

Simulations show adaptation efficiency comparable to neural gas, the strong clustering method identified in the abstract. The paper also proposes a nanostructure implementation described through a single-electron circuit. That proposal uses fluctuations arising from quantum tunneling as part of the computation itself. Together, the algorithm and hardware proposal connect a useful stochastic learning rule with a physical process capable of supplying its randomness.
neurips-2001-an-efficient-clustering-alg.tldr: Adding independent random fluctuations to online clustering comparisons yields efficient adaptation and motivates a single-electron hardware implementation.

paragraphs: Large stochastic control problems require decisions whose consequences unfold under uncertainty. Dynamic programming addresses such problems through a cost-to-go function, which describes future cost from a given situation. Computing that function exactly can become prohibitively expensive as the problem's dimensionality grows, motivating a more manageable approximation.

The paper studies a linear programming method that represents the cost-to-go function as a weighted combination of preselected basis functions. These functions provide the building blocks of the approximation, and the optimization fits their combination. This shifts the task from finding an unrestricted function to selecting a representation within a chosen family.

The authors develop bounds on approximation error and test the method on queueing network control. The bounds supply a theoretical way to assess approximation quality, while the experiments provide empirical support in a concrete control domain. Together, these contributions support linear programming as an efficient approach to approximate dynamic programming without claiming that the approximation solves every large control problem exactly.
neurips-2001-approximate-dynamic-program.tldr: Linear programming fits a compact cost-to-go approximation, supported by error bounds and queueing network control experiments.

paragraphs: This paper uses visible lip movements to help separate speech from noise recorded by a single microphone. The motivation is that visual speech cues can make noisy speech easier to understand. The proposed method targets non-stationary noise, where the interference changes over time and must be handled alongside the speech signal.

The authors extend speech enhancement methods based on hidden Markov models by incorporating lip information into a factorial combination of signal and noise models. They also introduce signal models with separate dynamics for narrow-band and wide-band components. This represents multiple evolving aspects of the recording, but combining them creates a potentially expensive inference problem.

A simple approximate inference method avoids the combinatorial growth of the factorial model and quickly estimates clean signals from the mixture. A preliminary evaluation on a small-vocabulary audiovisual database finds promising improvements in machine intelligibility. The evidence therefore supports the usefulness of combining sound and lip information in that evaluation, with the preliminary and limited-vocabulary setting remaining part of the claim.
neurips-2001-audio-visual-sound-separati.tldr: An audiovisual hidden Markov model uses lip movements to improve preliminary single-microphone speech separation results under changing noise.

paragraphs: The paper asks why dendrites tend to spread outward from a neuron's cell body despite showing local zigzags. A general preference for straight growth does not fully explain this organization. The authors examine two additional possibilities: dendrites may favor a fixed external direction, or they may be repelled by their own cell body.

They apply Bayesian analysis to reconstructed hippocampal neurons using a statistical model that linearly combines these two influences with a tendency to continue straight. Across all morphological classes examined, the estimated contribution of repulsion from the cell body is significantly positive and consistently exceeds the contribution of a fixed external direction.

When dendrites are artificially reoriented according to the model, the generated structures closely resemble real neuronal shapes. These findings suggest a role for somatodendritic repulsion rather than establishing a particular biological mechanism. Because neighboring hippocampal cells are densely packed and their dendrites overlap extensively, the proposed repulsion would need to distinguish a neuron's own cell body from those of other cells.
neurips-2001-bayesian-morphometry-of-hip.tldr: Bayesian analysis of neuronal shapes suggests that repulsion from a neuron's own cell body helps orient its dendrites.

paragraphs: This paper addresses classification when observations have many dimensions, labeled examples are scarce, and unlabeled examples are plentiful. It proposes learning the covariance kernel from the unlabeled task data. The kernel supplies the relationship between inputs used by methods such as support vector machines and Gaussian process classifiers.

The proposed mutual information kernel framework uses Bayesian generative models to construct this relationship. Its central idea is to let structure learned from available observations inform the representation used for classification. Unlabeled data can therefore contribute to the classifier's kernel even though those observations do not provide direct examples of the desired class assignments.

The authors describe an implementation based on variational Bayesian mixtures of factor analyzers. This is the concrete modeling machinery through which the framework addresses high-dimensional data. The contribution described in the abstract is a framework and implementation for making abundant unlabeled observations useful when labels are limited; it does not assert a particular measured improvement or a general superiority over other kernels.
neurips-2001-covariance-kernels-from-bay.tldr: Mutual information kernels use Bayesian generative models to learn classification kernels from abundant unlabeled data.

paragraphs: This paper asks where additional resources would most improve decision-making under uncertainty. Resources can include costly exploration, memory, computation, or a finer representation of the state space. The goal is to allocate them according to their expected effect on policy performance, rather than simply reducing uncertainty wherever it happens to be large.

The authors place exploration and adaptive discretization within a common Markov decision process framework. A current allocation defines beliefs over possible MDPs. Adding resources reduces uncertainty about some transition probabilities or rewards, so the central question becomes which uncertainty reduction is most likely to improve the resulting policy.

Sampling estimates how each parameter's probability distribution contributes to the expected loss from using an approximate policy instead of the true, unknown policy. One example of such an approximation is the optimal policy for the most probable MDP. This connects resource priorities to decision consequences and supplies a common basis for identifying valuable exploration regions or locations that merit additional grid points.
neurips-2001-efficient-resources-allocat.tldr: A sampling-based framework estimates where reducing MDP uncertainty is most likely to improve policy performance.

paragraphs: Estimating a discrete probability distribution becomes difficult when the observations undersample its possible outcomes. This paper examines popular near-uniform Dirichlet priors in that setting, specifically for discrete spaces without a metric. The issue is how assumptions about probabilities affect inference when the observations leave much of the distribution unresolved.

The authors show that these priors can produce disastrous results in the setting they study. They then use an Occam-style argument about phase space to expand the priors into an infinite mixture. The proposed remedy changes the prior construction itself, addressing problems associated with relying on the original near-uniform family in undersampled inference.

This mixture resolves most of the observed problems and produces an entropy estimator that the authors report as surprisingly good. Entropy is a summary of a distribution's uncertainty, so the contribution concerns both distribution learning and estimation of that summary. The stated result is a substantial improvement in the examined setting, with 'most' remaining an important qualification on how completely the prior-related problems are resolved.
neurips-2001-entropy-and-inference-revis.tldr: An infinite mixture of priors addresses most observed failures of near-uniform Dirichlet priors and yields a strong entropy estimator.

paragraphs: This paper studies Gaussian process regression when the learner's assumptions differ from the process generating the data. It derives approximations to learning curves, which describe how predictive performance changes as training examples accumulate. The distinction between the learner, called the student, and the generating process, called the teacher, makes model mismatch central to the analysis.

In the large-input-dimension regime where the results become exact, learning curves contain student-independent plateaux. Transitions between them can have arbitrarily many overfitting peaks. Correctly estimating the teacher's noise level does not necessarily prevent overfitting, showing that noise estimation alone does not remove the consequences of other mismatched assumptions.

Plateaux also occur in lower dimensions, where mismatch continues to affect learning even asymptotically. Excessively strong smoothness assumptions can be particularly damaging: a standard radial basis function covariance learns a rougher teacher function only logarithmically slowly in the stated example. Simulations confirm the predictions, supporting the conclusion that the relationship between model assumptions and the target function can shape learning throughout training.
neurips-2001-gaussian-process-regression.tldr: Mismatched Gaussian process assumptions can produce plateaux, repeated overfitting peaks, and extremely slow learning even with correct noise estimates.

paragraphs: People exposed to sentences from an artificial grammar can acquire implicit grammatical knowledge and transfer it to inputs produced by a modified grammar. This paper examines a related capability in a second-order recurrent neural network. The question is whether knowledge acquired from one structured language can remain useful when the language changes.

The authors demonstrate transfer from a language generated by a finite state machine to another language that differs in both vocabulary and syntax. This makes the demonstrated transfer broader than retaining knowledge when only the words change. The network carries useful grammatical knowledge across a setting in which both the symbols and their organization differ.

The paper also uses linear discriminant analysis to examine how the network represents grammatical knowledge. This adds an analysis of the learned representation to the behavioral demonstration of transfer. The result establishes the reported capability for the artificial-language setting studied, while the human findings provide the motivating phenomenon rather than proof that people and the network use the same mechanism.
neurips-2001-grammar-transfer-in-a-secon.tldr: A second-order recurrent network transfers grammatical knowledge between artificial languages that differ in vocabulary and syntax.

paragraphs: This paper studies belief propagation decoding, with particular attention to turbo decoding. The difficulty is that the belief network associated with turbo codes contains loops. In that setting, applying belief propagation does not make the true beliefs straightforward to obtain, and understanding the algorithm's behavior and equilibrium is itself a significant analytical problem.

The authors approach this problem through information geometry. This supplies a geometric viewpoint on probabilistic inference and a framework for examining what the decoder does. Their stated aim includes an intuitive account of the mechanism, so the framework is intended to clarify the decoding process as well as support formal analysis.

Using this viewpoint, the paper establishes basic properties of turbo decoding. The contribution is therefore an analytical explanation of an existing inference procedure and its equilibrium behavior. Its significance lies in making a difficult loopy decoding process more understandable and open to analysis; the abstract does not claim that the framework turns belief propagation into exact inference on these networks.
neurips-2001-information-geometrical-fra.tldr: Information geometry provides a framework for understanding belief propagation and basic properties of turbo decoding.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes decoding error in the belief propagation decoder for Gallager codes. It uses perturbation analysis and information geometry to identify the source of the principal error term at equilibrium. The focus is a specific leading contribution to error, rather than a claim about eliminating every possible decoding error.

The analysis connects that term to the m-embedding curvature of a log-linear submanifold. This geometric object is spanned by estimated pseudoposteriors: one representing the full marginal and additional partial posteriors that each account for a single parity check. The result relates the decoder's leading error to the geometry of the probability estimates it combines.

The authors then give a sufficient structural condition for this principal term to vanish. No two columns of the parity-check matrix may overlap in more than one position. This makes the significance of sparsity precise: the relevant requirement concerns how columns overlap, rather than merely how few entries are present overall. Under that condition, the identified leading error contribution disappears.
neurips-2001-information-geometrical-sig.tldr: A specific sparsity condition on Gallager codes makes the leading equilibrium decoding-error term vanish in an information-geometric analysis.

paragraphs: Kernel methods work with a feature-space representation whose dimension can track the number of training examples. Yet the data may occupy a smaller submanifold within that space. This paper develops a mathematical construction that adapts to this intrinsic dimension and finds an orthonormal basis for the smaller structure.

Representing the relevant structure through such a basis simplifies computations. The authors also use the construction as a theoretical foundation for kernelized blind source separation, the task of recovering hidden sources from mixtures. Their framework allows them to derive algorithms for arbitrary invertible nonlinear mixing, with invertibility being an explicit condition on the mixing process.

The paper presents kTDSEP as an algorithm arising from this approach. Experiments demonstrate good nonlinear source-separation performance and high computational efficiency. The contribution links a more economical representation of kernel-space data with a concrete inference task: adapting to the structure actually occupied by the data both simplifies the mathematics and supports an effective source-separation method in the reported experiments.
neurips-2001-kernel-feature-spaces-and-n.tldr: An intrinsic-dimensional kernel representation simplifies computation and supports efficient blind separation of invertible nonlinear mixtures.

paragraphs: This paper connects classification by logical formulas with classification by kernel machines. It asks both whether logical representations can be learned and how complex they must be to solve a classification problem. The connection creates a way to study symbolic rules through properties of a geometric learning representation.

The authors show that a special kernel can represent decision trees and disjunctive normal forms. They also link regularized risk to the separation margin, connecting an objective that accounts for prediction and regularization with the geometric separation of classes. This provides a bridge between the structure of logical classifiers and quantities studied in kernel learning.

The paper then derives several lower bounds on the complexity required of logical formulas. These bounds use properties of algorithms that generate linear estimators, including perceptron and maximal perceptron learning. Their significance is that they constrain how simple a successful logical solution can be, while the kernel representation provides the mathematical route for obtaining those constraints.
neurips-2001-kernel-machines-and-boolean.tldr: A kernel representation of logical classifiers connects margins and regularized risk to lower bounds on formula complexity.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational cost of learning low-dimensional features that preserve information useful for discrimination. An existing approach combines Renyi entropy with Parzen density estimation, but its computation grows quadratically with the number of training samples. That dependence makes using large training databases practically difficult.

The authors propose keeping the entropy-based approach while replacing Parzen estimation with a semiparametric density model, such as a Gaussian mixture model. This change allows all computation to occur in the low-dimensional target space. It also moves the quadratic dependence from the number of training samples to the number of mixture components.

The distinction matters because the size of the density representation becomes the quantity governing the stated quadratic cost. The paper further identifies a convenient extension to hidden Markov models of the kind used in speech recognition. Its contribution is thus a reformulation of the density-estimation machinery that makes discriminative feature learning more computationally manageable and opens a route to sequence-model applications.
neurips-2001-learning-discriminative-fea.tldr: Replacing Parzen density estimates with mixture models makes entropy-based feature learning operate in the low-dimensional target space.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational account of how animals combine information about the timing of stimuli during conditioning. Its starting point is the Temporal Coding Hypothesis, which proposes that related temporal patterns are integrated into a single memory representation. The emphasis is therefore on the organization of events in time, beyond simply recording that events are related.

The authors formalize this idea with a constrained hidden Markov model. They use quasi-Bayesian estimation to update the model's parameters as information is acquired. This turns a hypothesis about integrated temporal memory into a specified probabilistic learning approach whose behavior can be compared with conditioning results.

The approach accounts for some surprising temporal effects in the cited second-order conditioning experiments that other models cannot explain. The stated achievement concerns those effects, rather than every phenomenon in conditioning. Its importance is that explicitly representing and updating temporal structure gives the memory-integration hypothesis explanatory force in cases where the alternative models discussed fall short.
neurips-2001-modeling-temporal-structure.tldr: A constrained hidden Markov model formalizes integrated temporal memory and explains selected second-order conditioning effects.

paragraphs: This paper tests how attention changes spatial vision using simulations of interacting visual neurons. The model simultaneously predicts attention-related changes in visual thresholds across five dual-task human experiments. Its central explanation is that attention intensifies winner-take-all competition among early visual neurons within a cortical hypercolumn.

That hypothesis assumes attention affects all neurons equally and predicts both increased gain and sharper tuning. The abstract notes that each effect had been observed separately, but no single-unit study had demonstrated both together. This motivates testing whether changes in gain alone, distributed differently across neurons or tasks, could explain the behavioral data.

The alternatives amplify only the loudest, best-tuned, or most informative neurons, or amplify all neurons equally in a task-dependent way. None produces predictions as plausible as the intensified-competition account. The simulations therefore provide additional comparative support for that explanation. They do not establish that its two single-neuron predictions have been jointly observed, which remains the distinction motivating the alternative models.
neurips-2001-modeling-the-modulatory-eff.tldr: Simulations favor intensified neuronal competition over several gain-only explanations of attention's effects on spatial vision.

paragraphs: This paper models the firing of place and head-direction cells in rats by relating their spatial responses to environmental cues. It extends an earlier geometric model to include orientational information. The aim is a functional account of how features of the environment determine responses at both the individual-cell and population levels.

The model predicts responses when geometric and orientational cues are varied parametrically, meaning that particular aspects of those cues are adjusted in a controlled way. Combining the two cue types broadens the range of environmental manipulations the model addresses. It also generates quantitative predictions that the authors describe as readily testable.

The paper additionally considers remapping, which involves changes in firing that are not captured simply as parametric adjustments. This discussion suggests that the model may be compatible with such changes, while also placing constraints on future development. The distinction matters: predicting the stated controlled manipulations is a stronger claim than the proposed compatibility with remapping, which remains qualified.
neurips-2001-orientational-and-geometric.tldr: A spatial-cell model combines geometric and orientational cues to predict firing responses and may also accommodate remapping.

paragraphs: Factor analysis represents observations as linear combinations of normally distributed hidden variables. This paper generalizes that construction by allowing products of hidden variables to enter the representation. The resulting method, called product analysis, models observations as linear combinations of those products, introducing interactions into the relationship between hidden structure and observed data.

The authors describe the method as unsupervised linear regression on products of unobserved Gaussian variables. Although the combination of products is linear, the relationship to the underlying hidden variables is nonlinear. They therefore use an approximate variational method for both inference and learning, addressing the computational challenge introduced by this richer representation.

Because product analysis generalizes factor analysis, the paper states that it always finds a higher data likelihood. That is a claim about how well the model assigns probability to the data, distinct from a universal claim about task performance. The authors also present results on pattern recognition and image clustering that is invariant to illumination, illustrating applications of the nonlinear hidden-variable representation.
neurips-2001-product-analysis-learning-t.tldr: Product analysis extends factor analysis with products of Gaussian hidden variables to model nonlinear structure.

paragraphs: Moving through the world produces image motion that can reveal heading, but eye rotation, scene layout, and translation speed complicate that motion. Several visual models represent heading with neurons that respond to broad flow patterns. These detectors combine motion information from different image locations to infer the observer's direction of travel.

This paper analyzes those models to determine the precise receptive fields of their heading detectors. The authors ask which local motions contribute to a detector's response. This distinguishes the large-scale flow pattern associated with a heading from the directional preferences of the individual motion sensors supplying the detector.

Most analyzed models predict that the contributing sensors prefer motion arranged circularly around the detector's preferred heading, rather than radially. This challenges the widespread expectation described in the abstract. The results also suggest searching for finer organization within that circular structure, including bi-circularity and local motion opponency. These are consequences of the model analysis and directions for examining receptive fields, rather than reported direct observations of those structures in neurons.
neurips-2001-receptive-field-structure-o.tldr: Analysis of heading models predicts mostly circular, rather than radial, local motion preferences within heading detectors.

paragraphs: K-means groups observations by minimizing a sum of squared distances, commonly using coordinate descent to reach a local minimum. This paper reformulates that objective as a trace maximization problem involving the data's Gram matrix. The reformulation connects a familiar clustering objective with a matrix optimization problem.

The authors then relax the trace maximization problem. They show that this relaxed version has globally optimal solutions obtainable through a partial eigendecomposition of the Gram matrix. Cluster assignments are recovered using a pivoted QR decomposition of the eigenvector matrix, providing a sequence of matrix operations that leads from the relaxation to a partition.

The analysis also yields a lower bound on the minimum achievable sum-of-squares cost. This supplies theoretical information about the original clustering objective in addition to the assignment procedure. The central qualification is that the global optimality guarantee applies to the relaxed problem; it should not be read as a guarantee that every recovered discrete clustering globally minimizes the original K-means objective.
neurips-2001-spectral-relaxation-for-k-m.tldr: A spectral relaxation of K-means has globally optimal matrix solutions and yields cluster assignments plus a cost lower bound.

paragraphs: Applying support vector machines to speech requires a way to represent sequences of different lengths in a common classification space. This paper builds on the Fisher score, an established mapping for handling such data. Its contribution is a likelihood-ratio-based mapping that defines a different score-space for speech classification.

The new representation directly incorporates class-conditional generative models. In practical terms, the mapping draws on models associated with the classes being distinguished, making class-related probabilistic information part of the representation itself. The authors state that this construction avoids some limitations of the Fisher score and also examine appropriate normalization schemes.

The mapping is evaluated on speaker-independent recognition of isolated letters. In that task, it outperforms both the Fisher score and hidden Markov models trained by maximum likelihood. The result supports the proposed mapping as a useful bridge between generative sequence models and SVM classification in the tested setting. The comparison concerns the specified isolated-letter task, rather than an unrestricted claim about speech recognition generally.
neurips-2001-speech-recognition-using-sv.tldr: A likelihood-ratio score representation improves SVM recognition of isolated spoken letters over the tested Fisher-score and HMM alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper considers a restricted class of constrained minimum-divergence problems, which it calls generalized inference problems. Such problems combine an inference objective with requirements that the solution must satisfy. The authors address them by replacing the KL-divergence objective with an approximation based on Bethe free energy.

From that formulation they derive a unified propagation and scaling algorithm. Its updates are closely related to both loopy belief propagation and iterative scaling, bringing these procedures into one framework. This connection matters because the method addresses inference and constraints together through a shared optimization-based construction.

When the constraints are absent, the algorithm becomes a convergent alternative to loopy belief propagation. That is a specific convergence statement for the unconstrained case, rather than a claim of exact inference on arbitrary loopy models. Experiments demonstrate the algorithm's viability. The combined contribution is a method for the stated restricted problem class and a connection to a convergent inference procedure when the additional constraints are removed.
neurips-2001-the-unified-propagation-and.tldr: A Bethe-based algorithm unifies propagation and scaling, becoming a convergent alternative to loopy belief propagation without constraints.

paragraphs: This paper learns how an object's parts depend on one another from unlabeled observations, using moving human bodies as its examples. The input features contain both useful foreground parts and background clutter. Neither the relevant parts nor the correspondence between detected features and body parts is supplied in advance.

The method treats those unknown assignments as hidden variables and applies expectation-maximization. A greedy procedure selects parts and searches for a dependence structure using differential entropy. The authors represent probabilistic independence with decomposable triangulated graphs, while noting that their unsupervised technique is not restricted to that graph family.

This combination addresses two connected learning problems: deciding what the observations correspond to and discovering how the selected parts relate statistically. The authors demonstrate the algorithm by automatically generating human motion models from unlabeled real image sequences. The stated success shows that useful part-dependence models can be learned in those examples despite clutter and unknown assignments, without requiring manually labeled correspondences as training input.
neurips-2001-unsupervised-learning-of-hu.tldr: An unsupervised algorithm learns human motion dependencies from cluttered image sequences with unknown part assignments.
